I am completing my gun range and will have about 17 cubic yards of dirt in front of railroad ties and supported by layers of particle board. Using pvc to add strength to my shooting berm.

PVC is brittle, it's not going to explode but I bet one good hit would send cracks all down the length. If you have the want/ability to replace it occasionally, you can give it a shot.

Myself, personally, if I've got your design right in my head, you've basically got 17 yards of dirt on a pile, with a particle board... Backside?, I would drive a couple 4x4 posts in the ground, and use rope to secure them to the particle board so you can detach it for repair.

I went about it a different way. I had a bunch of cinder blocks left over from construction, so I built a 5 ft wall, filled it with mud, put two sheets of plywood on either side, and started filling them with dirt. At about halfway full, I lashed each sheet to the other with rope (So it kinda looks like a shoelace on each side) and pumped in enough water to make it mud. Filled up the other half, then dumped in some more water. The weight was pretty intense, and pulled the rope pretty damn tight. Didn't even have to put the plywood in the ground more than an inch or 3, just to initially keep it standing.

My end result is a solid wall of cinder block and mud with 2 sheets of easily replaceable plywood. Well. Easily replaceable the second time. The first time, you will probably have to cut the rope cause it'll be so tight and fused to the dirt.

Anyway. It stops my SKS. I wouldn't put it up against a .50, but I wouldn't put much up against that. Lol

Edit - for better imagining, the wall is about 3-3.5 FT thick, and just under 5Ftx5ft long/tall.

You should probably look at picking up a copy of the NRA Range Design Manual as it should supply you with a good amount of knowledge necessary to design an effective backstop.

You can supplement this with the Unified Facilities Code 4-023-07: Design to Resist Direct Fire Weapons Effects. which provides engineering calculations to determine ballistic penetration through various materials. This is more formulated towards building protection, but the principles are roughly the same.

PVC will shatter in one hit. What I did was go cut a small tree about 2-3" thick into sections about 4 ft tall. Use a digging bar to make a hole infront of your berm and drive the stakes into the dirt about every 2-3 ft leaving some further away and some closer to the berm. You can then wedge a log between the space you left for extra strength. My friend used an old pallet to stand his particle board up. This is sorta what I'm trying to describe https://www.google.com/amp/www.instructables.com/id/Wood-log-Shooting-Backstop/%3Famp_page%3Dtrue
You can build it cheap and fixit all the time or build it right and not.Grospoliner is right about the range design manual, and pvc is pretty weak when it comes to external forces.

My suggestion is to lean, multiple lengths, railroad ties backwards a few degrees, against the weight if the berm. If the berm starts pushing against the railroad ties, forcing them out, dig behind the ties and add another layer of ties as braces. You could also add railroad ties vertically in the corners for support.
